results.summary: This project implements a single two-input AND gate, with inputs in_a and in_b and output out. It is intended to be run in the Wokwi simulator, where toggling the inputs shows the AND result. No external hardware is required, and the documentation lists only placeholder text for external hardware. The design is a minimal logic-gate example, likely a first exercise, and no silicon test results are provided.

This design combines AND, NAND and OR gates driven by two inputs with a 16-stage flip-flop clock divider that produces divided outputs at the 12th and 16th stages. The eight outputs expose the gate results and the divided clock signals. It is tested by setting the inputs and checking that the outputs match the expected logic and timing. No external hardware is required beyond the simulator, and the project appears to be a student exercise in basic logic and sequential circuits.

This project generates an 8-bit chasing light pattern by dividing the 10 kHz clock down to 2.44 Hz and 0.3 Hz and using edge detection with flip-flops to sequence the outputs. The eight outputs are meant to drive LEDs through current-limiting resistors. It is tested by connecting LEDs to the output pins and observing the running pattern. The design is a simple educational demonstration of clock division and sequential logic.

This project is a first hands-on template copy with four input pins and four output pins. The documentation says only to toggle the input pins to create a value, and the same instruction is given for testing. No external hardware is needed. The design is essentially a passthrough or simple input-to-output mapping, and no further details or silicon results are provided.

This project is described as a 7-segment display template copy, with eight inputs and eight outputs. The only usage instruction is to press a switch, and the external hardware section says the author does not know what to do. There is no explanation of how the display is driven or what the outputs represent. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual function beyond a possible switch-to-display mapping.

This project connects two inputs to an AND gate and also passes one input directly to an output, with additional unspecified outputs. The documentation is filled with placeholder text and does not explain the design or how to test it. No external hardware is described. The project appears to be an incomplete or joke submission with no meaningful technical content.

This design uses the clock to drive a rotating pattern on a 7-segment display, looping through states and possibly requiring a few seconds to reset from undefined flip-flop states. It is intended to be run without specific tests, and it needs an external PMOD 7-segment display. The documentation is minimal and notes that no tests have been performed yet. The project is a simple demonstration of sequential logic driving a display.

This project aims to display numbers from 0 to 9 on an 8-segment display, with eight inputs, eight bidirectional pins and eight outputs. It is tested using buttons, and external hardware consists of eight buttons. The documentation is very sparse, saying only 'sign numbers' and 'buttons', so the exact mapping and control scheme are unclear. The design appears to be a student exercise in driving a display with button inputs.

This project is a test of the tapeout process itself, with eight inputs and eight outputs. The documentation is circular, stating that it works by working and can be used by using it. No external hardware is mentioned. It is essentially a placeholder or process test with no functional design described.

This project has no meaningful documentation, with all fields filled with the German word 'Pfusch' (botch) repeated. The pin names are all 'abc', and no function or test procedure is described. No external hardware is specified. The design is effectively undocumented and appears to be a non-serious submission.
